did_you_know.text: Isaac can no longer see well, so he must rely on hearing, touch, and smell. Much of the chapter turns on which sense will reveal the truth.
In the biblical world, a blessing from an elderly father was more than a kind wish; it declared a son’s status and future.
Goats were common domesticated animals in the region and provided milk, meat, and leather. That made them a practical source for a quick meal resembling hunters’ food.
Esau’s clothes are described as special or valuable garments. Their smell was meant to make Jacob’s disguise more convincing.
Goat skins are covered with coarse hair, so they could fool someone checking by touch whether the person was Esau.
The phrase “God caused it to happen” can also mean “God arranged it.” Jacob presents his success as something brought about by God.
The line “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands” is a clear example of biblical parallelism, contrasting sound with touch.
Smell is given a meaning of natural abundance in the blessing. The fertile field becomes a symbol of a blessed land.
In the land, where summers are dry and rain is seasonal, dew had real agricultural value. That is why “the dew of heaven” symbolizes blessing and fertility.

The end of the blessing echoes God’s promise to Abraham in Genesis 12: “Those who bless you will be blessed, and those who curse you will be cursed.” Isaac’s blessing is thus linked to the promise given to the previous generation.
After realizing what happened, Isaac says, “Indeed, he shall remain blessed.” He appears to regard the blessing already spoken as binding and not easily revoked.

Esau plays on the similarity between the name Jacob and the Hebrew root עק״ב, associated with a heel and with outmaneuvering or deceiving. It is a wordplay, not a scientific explanation of the name’s origin.

The phrase “when you grow restless” is ambiguous, so it has been interpreted in different ways, such as “when you rebel” or “when you exert yourself.” This ambiguity makes the end of the blessing complex.
Haran was an ancient city in northern Mesopotamia, in what is now southeastern Turkey. It was an important center on trade routes between Mesopotamia and the Levant.

The Hittites were an important people of the ancient Near East, centered in Anatolia. Mentioning the daughters of Heth also expresses concern about marriages that might distance the family from its traditions.
